newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank meets to set M3 money supply target.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank meets to set M3 money supply target.

text.p: The policy-making council of Germany's Bundesbank met on Thursday to set its money supply target for 1997, with economists seeing very little chance that the decision would be accompanied by an interest rate cut.

The Bundesbank traditionally sets a one-year target for growth in M3 money supply in the following year just before its Christmas break. It argues that M3 is the best guide to future inflation in the economy and so to interest rate policy needs.
But some economists believe the central bank will break with that tradition this year and set a two-year target.
This would allow the central bank to bridge the period to the end of 1998, when the European central bank will take over responsibility for monetary policy in Europe.
Others predict that the Bundesbank will stick with its policy of setting a formal one-year target, but add in an extra element to show how it thinks the money supply should develop in 1998.
The bank's chief economist Otmar Issing has already said that the Bundesbank will look ahead to the transfer of monetary policy power to the ECB when it sets its target this Thursday.

The meeting will be followed by a news conference, scheduled for 1300 GMT. Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer is chairing the meeting, which will also be attended by Juergen Stark, state secretary to the German finance ministry.

The Bundesbank traditionally compiles its M3 target by looking at likely developments in growth and prices, making adjustments for changes in the way in which money is being used, and then placing a target corridor around its central estimate of M3 growth needs.

For 1996, it set a corridor of four to six percent, based on an assessment of production potential at 2.5 percent, unavoidable inflation of two percent and a one percent element to compensate for slower velocity of circulation of money.
Velocity of circulation is a measure of how intensively funds are used in the economy.
From the central figure of 5.5 percent, the central bank created a corridor of four to seven percent.
Regardless of whether a two-year or one-year target is set this year, economists expect the methodology to be the same, and say the underlying assumptions will also be similar.

Among those economists polled, eight said they expected the target to be set on Thursday to be unchanged from 1996, and seven expected a slightly lower growth range. The other three gave only a central expansion rate not a target range.

Almost all of the economists polled expected the central bank to hold its leading interest rates steady at this week's meeting, with a minority predicting that the central bank would trim its three percent money market rate slightly.
